title: DHCP
summary: How a new device gets an address, mask, gateway and DNS server without anyone typing them.

steps.title: DORA
body: A host with no address can't send unicast, so DHCP starts with broadcasts (UDP 67/68):
| <-- ACK ---------------------------- |  "it's yours: mask, router, DNS, lease"
The **lease** has an expiry. At 50% (T1) the client renews with its server; at 87.5% (T2) it asks any server; at 100% it must stop using the address.
Options deliver the rest: subnet mask, default **router**, **DNS** servers, domain name, NTP.
> **Practise for real:** **Labs → Live network labs** runs real Linux hosts, switches and routers you can poke at.

steps.prompt: A lease lasts 86400 seconds. When does the client try to renew (T1 = 50%) and rebind (T2 = 87.5%)?
steps.explain: Renewing early means a short server outage doesn't take every host offline.

steps.prompt: Match each DHCP option to what it gives the client.
A laptop shows `169.254.37.12` and has no internet. What does that mean?
options: It never got a DHCP reply and gave itself a link-local address
steps.explain: APIPA/link-local means DHCP failed: check the cable/VLAN, the server, or the relay.

steps.title: Relays and rogue servers
body: Broadcasts don't cross routers, so one central DHCP server serves many subnets through a **relay agent** on each router
(`ip helper-address` on Cisco). The relay forwards the request as unicast and tells the server which subnet it came from (`giaddr`), so the server picks the right pool.
Anyone can answer a DISCOVER. A **rogue DHCP server** (a misplugged home router, or an attacker) hands out its own gateway and DNS, putting itself in the middle.
Switches defend with **DHCP snooping**: only trusted ports may send OFFERs and ACKs.

steps.prompt: Half the office suddenly gets addresses in `192.168.0.x` instead of `10.20.0.x`, with gateway `192.168.0.1`. Most likely?
options: A rogue DHCP server, e.g. someone plugged in a consumer router; enable DHCP snooping and find its port
The DHCP server ran out of addresses
steps.explain: Clients take the first offer. `192.168.0.1` is a typical home router default.

steps.prompt: Complete: release the current lease, then request a new one with verbose output, on Linux.
steps.explain: On Windows the same is `ipconfig /release` then `ipconfig /renew`.

steps.title: A DHCP server
prompt: Write a class `DhcpServer` constructed with the first and last address of its pool:
- `string? Discover(string mac)`: offers (and reserves) the address this MAC already has, else the **lowest** free address, else `null` (pool exhausted).
- `string Request(string mac, string ip)`: `"ACK"` if `ip` is reserved for this MAC, else `"NAK"`.
solution: private readonly Dictionary<string, uint> leases = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
public DhcpServer(string first, string last) { this.first = ToU(first); this.last = ToU(last); }
static uint ToU(string ip) => ip.Split('.').Aggregate(0u, (acc, o) => (acc << 8) | uint.Parse(o));
if (leases.TryGetValue(mac, out uint ip)) return FromU(ip);
for (uint a = first; a <= last; a++)
public string Request(string mac, string ip) => leases.TryGetValue(mac, out uint a) && FromU(a) == ip ? "ACK" : "NAK";
template: Dojo.Eq("same MAC gets the same address", "10.0.0.10", dojoD.Discover("AA:00:00:00:00:01"));
Dojo.Eq("NAK for someone else's address", "NAK", dojoD.Request("aa:00:00:00:00:02", "10.0.0.10"));
hints: Store `mac -> address` as a `uint`; addresses are easy to loop over as numbers.
Lowest free: loop from first to last, skipping used ones.
